items.title: Report: AI accelerates software development but increases complexity and risks eroding middle-class engineering roles by 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI is removing the middle class of software engineering?
items.summary:
A 2026 report describes how AI tools have dramatically increased the speed of software development, enabling large code changes and rapid feature additions. However, this acceleration has led to deteriorating code quality, convoluted systems, and reliance on AI for understanding and fixing issues, undermining traditional engineering practices and oversight.

The report illustrates a scenario where engineers struggle to comprehend AI-generated code changes, leading to fragile projects that are difficult to maintain or justify fixing. It highlights the challenges teams face in managing AI-driven development, including the loss of clear architectural understanding and the inability to hold engineers accountable for design decisions.

This trend suggests that the role of middle-class software engineers, who traditionally ensured code quality and system coherence, is at risk as AI tools enable less experienced developers to produce large volumes of code without sufficient oversight. The report warns that without strong engineering culture and discipline, AI may accelerate project failures and complicate software maintenance.

items.title: Google launches Pixel Watch 5 with Gemini AI for proactive assistance and advanced health tracking, including emergency breathing detection and improved GPS, available August 20 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Pixel Watch 5: Proactive assistance and advanced health tracking on your wrist
items.summary:
Google has introduced the Pixel Watch 5, featuring Gemini Intelligence for hands-free, proactive assistance and enhanced health tracking capabilities. The watch offers the most accurate GPS tracking yet, even in challenging environments, and debuts Health Guardian tools such as breathing emergency detection and monthly wellness summaries for blood pressure, sleep, and metabolic health. Pre-orders began on August 12, with general availability starting August 20.

Powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 processor and increased RAM, the Pixel Watch 5 delivers faster performance and low-latency AI interactions, including quick access to calendar events and workout controls through intuitive gestures. The device integrates advanced environmental modeling and real-time atmospheric data to improve location accuracy, supporting users in both urban and trail settings.

These enhancements aim to provide users with seamless, context-aware updates and health insights directly on their wrist, enabling better management of daily tasks and fitness. The Pixel Watch 5 builds on its predecessor's design and capabilities to offer a more responsive and health-focused smartwatch experience.

items.title: X.ai releases Grok 4.6 with enhanced long-running agent capabilities and improved interactive and visual project performance, matching GPT-5.6 Sol on key AI benchmarks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Grok 4.6
items.summary:
X.ai has launched Grok 4.6, an update focused on supporting long-running AI agents and more complex interactive and visual tasks. The model matches GPT-5.6 Sol on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, a composite of nine benchmarks, and is available through Cursor, Grok Build, and API partners like OpenRouter, Vercel, and Cloudflare. The release includes a twofold increase in included usage for the first week to encourage adoption.

Grok 4.6 underwent extended training with curated data emphasizing reasoning, technical concepts, and engineering tasks, resulting in improved performance and behavior. It excels at transforming broad product ideas into working prototypes, including research, structuring, implementation, and iterative refinement, with enhanced self-testing and verification on longer tasks. Visual and interactive project outputs have also improved significantly compared to the previous version.

Safety measures have been upgraded to align with the model's expanded capabilities, supporting secure use cases such as vulnerability patching and AI research augmentation. The release includes comprehensive pre-deployment and post-deployment testing to ensure balanced utility and security. Pricing starts at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens, with a faster variant available at double the price.

items.title: Researchers quantify routing-induced performance degradation in quantized Top-k Mixture-of-Experts models, finding about one-third of damage from 4-bit KV-cache quantization is due to routing flips [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Detecting a Route Flip Is Easier Than Knowing Whether to Fix It: Causal Route-Mediated Damage in Quantized Mixture-of-Experts
items.summary: This study examines how numerical disturbances from 4-bit key-value cache quantization affect routing decisions in Top-k Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, causing tokens to switch activated experts and degrade performance. The researchers developed a causal framework and empirical methods to measure the fraction of performance loss attributable to these routing flips, finding that roughly 31% of the damage is routing-mediated across multiple architectures. While the system can detect when a routing flip occurs, it cannot reliably determine if the flip is beneficial or harmful based on local router statistics, highlighting challenges in selectively repairing such errors. The findings were validated through pre-registered experiments and consistent across different model architectures, providing insights into the limitations of current detection and mitigation approaches for routing-induced quantization damage in MoE models.
items.description: This study examines how numerical disturbances from 4-bit key-value cache quantization affect routing decisions in Top-k Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, causing tokens to switch activated experts and degrade performance. The researchers developed a causal framework and empirical methods to measure the fraction of performance loss attributable to these routing flips, finding that roughly 31% of the damage is routing-mediated across multiple architectures. While the system can detect when a routing flip occurs, it cannot reliably determine if the flip is beneficial or harmful based on local router statistics, highlighting challenges in selectively repairing such errors. The findings were validated through pre-registered experiments and consistent across different model architectures, providing insights into the limitations of current detection and mitigation approaches for routing-induced quantization damage in MoE models.
items.originalSummary: The paper investigates the effects of quantization-induced routing changes in Top-k Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, specifically focusing on how numerical disturbances can cause tokens to switch which experts are activated. The study introduces a causal framework and empirical methods to quantify the fraction of performance degradation attributable to routing changes. Findings indicate that approximately one-third of the damage from 4-bit key-value cache quantization is due to routing flips. While the system can detect when a routing flip occurs, it cannot reliably determine whether the flip is beneficial or harmful based on local router statistics. These results were consistent across multiple architectures and were validated through pre-registered experiments. The research highlights challenges in selectively repairing routing-induced errors and provides insights into the limitations of current detection methods.

items.title: Researchers develop low-parameter surrogate models to simulate large LLM-agent societies efficiently on a laptop, validated across multiple simulations with predicted error trends [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Poor Man's Agentic Modeling: Simulating Large LLM-Agent Societies on a Laptop
items.summary: Researchers have created a method to simulate large societies of language model agents by replacing each agent with a low-parameter model derived from a few hundred to a few thousand inexpensive queries. This approach focuses on macroscopic behaviors rather than individual agent cognition and uses a taxonomy based on interaction order and memory to predict simulation errors. The method was validated on a reimplementation of the LLM macroeconomy EconAgent and seven other simulations, showing accurate error trend predictions without free parameters. This technique enables running large-scale LLM-agent simulations on standard laptops, significantly reducing computational costs while maintaining fidelity to key simulation outcomes.

items.title: Researchers present SAPO, a segment-level automatic prompt optimization method that decomposes prompts for targeted improvements, outperforming zero-shot and strong APO baselines on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Monolithic to Modular: Segment-level Automatic Prompt Optimization
items.summary: SAPO introduces a modular approach to automatic prompt optimization by breaking prompts into segments such as role, context, tasks, and output format, then applying targeted improvements based on analysis of top and bottom performing examples. The method uses a single large language model with static meta-prompts to perform segmentation, diagnose weaknesses, and generate candidate improvements. Evaluations on benchmarks including SQuADv2, TweetEval, XSUM, CommonGen, and GSM8K with GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4o-mini demonstrate that SAPO achieves better average scores compared to zero-shot prompting and several strong APO baselines. This approach addresses limitations of traditional monolithic prompt rewriting, which can improve some behaviors while degrading others.

items.title: Researchers find majority vote self-consistency reduces accuracy on most hard science problems for small instruction-tuned LLMs Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3-8B [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Self-Consistency Backfires: Majority Vote Hurts the Majority of Hard Science Problems for Small LLMs
items.summary: A study on the GPQA Diamond benchmark of 198 graduate-level science questions shows that using majority vote self-consistency decreases per-problem accuracy for 56.6% of problems with Qwen2.5-7B and 65.7% with Llama-3-8B. The effect was confirmed on a pre-registered 151-problem split and suggests confidence scores do not reliably indicate correctness for these models. An oracle method selecting the best number of samples per problem could improve accuracy by up to 17 points, but no practical verifier-free gating method achieved this. The research highlights limitations of majority voting in small instruction-tuned models and leaves open the question of its impact on reasoning-native models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-consistency (SC) via majority vote is a widely used way to spend inference-time compute: sample N chains of thought, return the plurality answer. On the full GPQA Diamond benchmark (198 graduate-level science questions), majority voting reduces per-problem accuracy on a majority of problems for two instruction-tuned models from different families: 56.6% of problems for Qwen2.5-7B and 65.7% for Llama-3-8B, with Qwen the primary demonstration and Llama corroborating the direction from a near-chance baseline. The effect was pre-registered on a 151-problem confirmatory split after being observed on 47 exploratory problems, and all four confirmatory hypotheses passed. A grid oracle that routes each problem to the best N across {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64} marks a theoretical upper bound 14 accuracy points above N = 1 for Qwen and 17 for Llama, an oracle bound requiring ground truth rather than a deployable method. No verifier-free gate reaches it: neither a plurality-agreement gate nor a token-entropy gate moves accuracy more than 0.002 from fixed-budget voting at N = 64. The mechanism is direct: confidence does not track correctness on these problems. In the highest-agreement bin the plurality answer is correct about half the time for Qwen, and for Llama that bin is less accurate than its lowest-agreement bin. We pre-register and confirm these findings on small instruction-tuned models; we do not test reasoning-native models, which we flag as the central open question.

items.title: Mechanist uses AI to autonomously discover mechanisms of intelligence, integrating a large knowledge graph and multidisciplinary database to generate hypotheses and conduct experiments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Mechanist: AI as a Scientific Instrument for Discovering the Mechanisms of Intelligence
items.summary:
Mechanist is an AI-driven system designed to autonomously uncover the mechanisms behind AI intelligence by leveraging a knowledge graph of 13,000 papers and a multidisciplinary database of 43 million papers across 26 fields. It incorporates 32 foundational methods for mechanism analysis, causal intervention, and validation, outperforming existing AI-scientist systems in hypothesis generation and experiment execution.

The system progresses from identifying model behaviors to explaining and controlling AI models, revealing a safety risk where unsafe traits transfer across modalities via safe training data. Mechanist also develops a theory of belief explaining how models represent knowledge and form beliefs during pretraining. These insights enable practical interventions that enhance model performance and guide scientific foundation models to generate DNA sequences with specified properties.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI models have achieved remarkable success across diverse domains, yet the mechanisms underlying their capabilities and the risks they may pose remain poorly understood. As AI development becomes faster and increasingly automated, mechanistic exploration remains largely manual, widening the gap between what models can do and our ability to understand and control them. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mechanist, an agentic system that uses AI as a scientific instrument for the autonomous discovery of mechanisms underlying AI intelligence. To support autonomous mechanistic discovery, we construct an interpretability-focused knowledge graph of approximately 13,000 papers and integrate it with a multidisciplinary database of 43 million papers spanning 26 fields. We further curate a library of 32 foundational methods for mechanism analysis, causal intervention, and validation. Compared with Claude Code and existing AI-scientist systems, Mechanist generates more valuable mechanism hypotheses and executes experiments more reliably. Mechanist also demonstrates a progression from discovering model behaviors to explaining and controlling AI models. Specifically, Mechanist first uncovers a counterintuitive safety risk in scientific laboratories, showing that unsafe traits can transfer across modalities through apparently safe training data. Mechanist then develops a mechanism theory of belief, revealing how models represent world knowledge, form beliefs, infer the beliefs of others, and how these mechanisms emerge during pretraining. Finally, Mechanist translates these mechanistic insights into practical interventions that improve model performance across diverse scenarios and steer scientific foundation models toward generating DNA sequences with specified properties.

items.title: Researchers retrofit recurrent depth into pretrained Qwen2.5-0.5B language model, demonstrating iterative latent transitions and improved reasoning at two parameter budgets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Retrofitting Recurrent Depth into a Pretrained Language Model: Installation, Extrapolation, Transfer, and Retention at Two Parameter Budgets
items.summary:
Researchers have retrofitted recurrent depth into the pretrained Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct language model by splitting it into a Prelude, a weight-tied Recurrent Block, and a Coda, enabling iterative latent transitions that persist after outcome-only annealing. The retrofit operates at two parameter budgets—6 million trained parameters over frozen base weights and 180 million full-block parameters—and matches or exceeds the base model's performance on a preregistered ARC benchmark, with improved reasoning depth and speed compared to scratchpad-trained models.
The study found that the recurrent mechanism functions as a reusable procedure rather than a terminal-answer lookup, extrapolates to about 1.5 times its supervised depth while maintaining accuracy, and supports verbal fine-tuning with better transfer than fresh training. However, attempts to learn inverse operations while preserving the installed mechanism revealed catastrophic interference, indicating limits to the approach. The work suggests iterative transformers can perform deeper reasoning in latent space more efficiently than comparable or larger fine-tuned models, though learned depth selection remains an open challenge.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A dense, pretrained language model can be retrofitted with recurrent depth and learn an iterative latent transition that persists after outcome-only annealing. Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct is split into a Prelude, a weight-tied Recurrent Block, and a Coda, with an identity-preserving one-loop path and a re-entry bridge on later loops. At loop 1 the retrofit remains non-inferior to its base on a preregistered ARC battery. Three findings. First, the mechanism is a reusable procedure rather than terminal-answer lookup, and installs at two budgets: 6M trained parameters over frozen base weights and 180M full-block. With intermediate-step supervision, the model computes one task step per loop and persists when only final answers are graded. The adapter matched the full block overall (83.8% versus 84.0%), led through depth 11, and trailed beyond. Verbal fine-tuning reached 79-86% on controlled verbal renderings (zero-shot transfer was minimal), and adapter verbal training begun from the installed mechanism outpaced matched fresh training by 18.6 points, including on a held-out test set. Second, the operation extrapolates to roughly 1.5 times its supervised depth, holding 70% accuracy through depth 18. Third, a same-size scratchpad-trained model matched the recurrent model within its learned horizon but collapsed beyond it. The recurrent model won overall, 84% versus 72%, retained 53% versus 2.5% beyond depth 10, and answered 7.6 times faster. An iterative transformer can therefore perform deeper reasoning in latent space faster than comparable or larger models fine-tuned on the same task, in a system-level comparison. A second task, running the rule in reverse, exposed the limits: the inverse was learnable in isolation, but no continuation acquired it while preserving the installed mechanism and general capability, a catastrophic-interference boundary. Learned depth selection remains open.

items.originalTitle: Diffuse to Compress: Leveraging Diffusion LMs for Lossless Compression
items.summary: Researchers propose using Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) as an alternative to autoregressive large language models for lossless text compression, aiming to overcome throughput limitations inherent in one-symbol-per-step inference. They develop strategies to address algorithmic challenges unique to DLMs and evaluate their approach on the enwik8 benchmark, demonstrating improved compression performance compared to existing neural and general-purpose compressors. The study highlights the potential for further enhancements as DLMs continue to evolve as a relatively new modeling paradigm.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11249v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of lossless text compression, motivated by the rapid growth in the collection and storage of digital textual data - including plain text, source code, and structured formats such as XML - and by recent advances in neural language model-based compression. In particular, recent LLM-based approaches, whether built on symbol-ranking pipelines or paired with a statistical compressor, have demonstrated compression ratios significantly superior to general-purpose compressors such as zstd, gzip, or bzip on text and code. However, these neural approaches suffer from severe throughput limitations, making them not yet practically usable. For the first time in the context of lossless neural text compression, we introduce Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) as an alternative inference paradigm to autoregressive LLM-based approaches. We argue that replacing autoregressive LLMs with DLMs within the same compression framework could overcome the throughput bottleneck caused by their one-symbol-per-step limitation. However, achieving these improvements requires addressing algorithmic challenges introduced by applying DLMs to lossless compression, where the architecture allows the number and positions of symbols encoded at each forward pass to be decided independently. We design efficient and effective strategies to solve these challenges and evaluate them experimentally against LLM-based and general-purpose compressors on enwik8, a well-established textual benchmark. Our results show that the newly proposed DLM-based framework advances the state of the art in lossless text compression. Moreover, as DLMs are still a relatively young paradigm, recent advances toward increasingly capable and efficient models suggest substantial room for further improvements.

items.title: Researchers evaluate uncertainty quantification methods for LLM agents across multi-turn trajectories, finding uneven transfer from single-turn approaches and highlighting the importance of consistency measurement and aggregator choice [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Single-Turn Confidence: Trajectory-Adapted Uncertainty Quantification for LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers studied how uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods developed for single-turn language model outputs perform when applied to multi-turn interactive trajectories of large language model (LLM) agents. They evaluated three families of UQ methods—white-box token-probability scorers, black-box consistency scorers, and reflexive self-assessment scorers—across five LLMs and four multi-turn tool-use datasets. The study found that while some single-turn UQ methods transfer usefully to multi-turn settings, their effectiveness varies significantly depending on the method and aggregation approach used across turns.

The results showed that token-probability scores are highly sensitive to the choice of aggregator, reflexive self-assessment provides a strong low-cost baseline in most cases, and black-box self-consistency methods often perform best, particularly variants measuring trajectory-equivalence and action-set consistency. These findings suggest that UQ methods should be revalidated at the trajectory level for LLM agents, with careful consideration of consistency metrics, aggregation strategies, and computational costs to improve uncertainty estimation in multi-turn interactions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods for language models are typically evaluated on single-turn outputs, where uncertainty is attached to one generated answer. For LLM agents, however, the unit of observation is an interactive trajectory, where the model can ask clarifying questions, call tools, update state, and make intermediate decisions whose errors propagate to the final outcome. We study whether three common families of single-turn UQ methods transfer to this setting. Across five LLMs and four multi-turn tool-use datasets from BFCL-v4 and $\tau^2$-bench, we evaluate white-box scorers based on action-token probabilities, black-box consistency scorers based on resampled trajectories, and reflexive scorers based on model self-assessment of the trajectory. We find that transfer is often useful but uneven. Token-probability scores are highly sensitive to the choice of aggregator used across turns, reflexive scores provide the strongest low-cost baseline in most evaluated settings, and black-box self-consistency is often the strongest UQ family, with trajectory-equivalence and action-set consistency typically ranking highest among its variants. These results suggest that UQ methods developed for single generations should be revalidated at the trajectory level, with careful attention to the consistency measurement, aggregator choice, and computational budget.

items.title: Researchers propose Hybrid-Policy Self-Editing (HPSE) to improve composable unstructured knowledge editing in large language models by combining on-policy and off-policy learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Hybrid-Policy Self-Editing for Composable Unstructured Knowledge Editing
items.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) struggle to update specific knowledge without affecting unrelated information, especially when edits involve unstructured passages containing multiple facts. Researchers identify that existing knowledge editors fail to enable models to answer detailed questions or perform multi-hop reasoning on edited content due to passive reliance on the fixed passage as the sole learning source. To address this, they introduce Hybrid-Policy Self-Editing (HPSE), which proactively distills knowledge by combining the model's own trajectories with targeted insertions of missing facts, enhancing the model's ability to integrate new information effectively without external supervision.

HPSE builds a hybrid rollout that supplements the model's on-policy learning with off-policy steps precisely where the model's coverage of new knowledge is lacking. The approach is theoretically analyzed and empirically validated across four LLM architectures and two knowledge editing editors, demonstrating plug-and-play improvements in various scenarios. This method aims to advance the composability of knowledge edits, enabling LLMs to better recall and reason about updated information in dynamic environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11660v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable performance across natural language tasks, yet they are trained on static corpora and their knowledge quickly becomes outdated in a fast-changing world. This motivates knowledge editing (KE), which updates specific knowledge in an LLM without changing unrelated others. Recent works move from structured knowledge triples toward unstructured KE (UKE), where the edit is a free-form passage that may state multiple facts at once. Nonetheless, existing editors inject such a passage yet fail to use it: the edited model can recall the passage, but can neither answer atomic questions about its facts nor compose them into multi-hop reasoning. We attribute this missing property, which we term composability, to editors' passive reliance on the fixed passage as the sole learning source. In response, we cast editing as a proactive self-distillation from a privileged in-context state of the same model, which requires no external supervision. We further reveal that due to the novelty of the injected knowledge, the pre-edited model's own rollouts rarely cover it, which limits the effectiveness of pure on-policy distillation. To close this gap, we propose HPSE, which builds a hybrid rollout that steps in to place missing facts onto the student's own trajectory precisely where its coverage fails, while staying on-policy elsewhere. We theoretically analyze HPSE's advantage over pure on-policy distillation, and empirically establish its plug-and-play improvements across four LLM backbones and two KE editors under various scenarios.

items.title: Researchers propose Rubric Dropout to reduce reward hacking in reinforcement learning with LLM-graded rubrics, improving out-of-distribution performance on medical and science benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-as-Reward RL
items.summary: Researchers identify reward hacking in reinforcement learning against fixed rubrics graded by large language model judges, where policies exploit rubric limitations leading to divergence between training and gold judge scores. They introduce Rubric Dropout, a method that randomly drops subsets of rubric criteria during training to prevent overfitting to fixed rubrics while maintaining evaluation on the full rubric. Experiments with Qwen3-8B and Group Relative Policy Optimization on medical and science tasks show that Rubric Dropout improves out-of-distribution benchmark scores by up to 7 points and reduces reward hacking without domain performance loss. The study finds a 30-50% dropout rate optimal and notes that reweighting criteria by training usefulness performs worse than no intervention.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning against rubrics, lists of criteria graded by an LLM judge, has become a standard way to post-train language models on tasks with no deterministic answer. The rubric, however, is a fixed proxy for quality, never a complete description of it, and a policy trained against it long enough will learn to exploit the difference. We measure this directly. Training Qwen3-8B with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on medical and science rubrics and grading out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks with both the training judge and a stronger gold judge, we find that the two scores diverge during training. The training judge's score keeps climbing while the gold judge's score peaks and then falls, by 3 points on HealthBench-Hard and by 22 points on ResearchQA. A judge with a fixed bias would shift the gold curve by a constant, not send it down while the training score rises, so the divergence is reward hacking, not judge noise. We propose Rubric Dropout, a one-line fix borrowed from neuron dropout. At every step, we randomly drop a subset of the rubric's criteria before computing the reward, so the policy never optimizes the same rubric twice. The dropped subset is shared across each rollout group, so GRPO's group-relative advantages stay comparable, and evaluation always uses the full rubric. Comparing no dropout against dropout at 30% and 50% on both benchmark pairs, dropout raises the OOD gold score at every matched checkpoint (+1 to +2 points on HealthBench-Hard, +6 to +7 points on ResearchQA), lowers the two hacking measures we track, and costs nothing in domain. Sweeping the dropout fraction shows a broad 30-50% sweet spot, while the natural alternative, reweighting criteria by how useful they are to training, performs worse than no intervention at all in our setting.

items.title: Researchers identify and control internal activation signals linked to implicit demographic personalization in five large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Locating and Controlling Implicit Personalization in Large Language Models
items.summary: Researchers analyzed five large language models and found that implicit demographic cues trigger localized internal activation signals correlated with changes in model outputs. They demonstrated that removing these internal signals can suppress the influence of specific demographic cues more effectively than prompting the model to ignore demographics, while maintaining overall benchmark performance. The study reveals that the ability to selectively control these signals varies by model and attribute, connecting implicit personalization behavior to internal mechanisms that can be causally manipulated.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often shift their outputs in response to implicit demographic cues even when users never state a demographic identity. Previous work has documented this behavior, but the connection between these behavioral changes and the model's internal activations remains unclear. Using matched cued and neutral conversations across five LLMs, we establish that a localized internal activation signal tracks changes in recommendations, with correlations up to r=0.87. When multiple cues appear together, their internal signals largely combine, but the changes in output do not simply add up. We further show that removing the internal signal associated with one cue can suppress its influence, often more effectively than asking the model to ignore demographics via prompting, while largely preserving general benchmark performance. However, the ability to selectively remove one dimension's influence while leaving co-present dimensions intact remains highly model- and attribute-specific. These results connect implicit personalization behavior to an internal signal that can be analyzed and causally controlled.

items.originalTitle: GRPO for Financial Advice Generation: Outperforming Commercial LLMs under CATE Evaluation
items.summary: Researchers developed a method to generate actionable financial advice by fine-tuning an open-weight language model using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a reward system based on an LLM-as-a-judge rubric and a safety gate to prevent harmful recommendations. They complemented this evaluation with a judge-independent audit using a doubly-robust Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) estimator to measure genuine business value. Their trained model achieved roughly twice the estimated gross-profit lift of the best commercial baseline, with lower downside risk and negative tail risk. The study highlights that GRPO with finance-grounded rewards can produce more useful business recommendations than commercial LLMs and that causal audits provide valuable complementary evaluation beyond LLM-based judging.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generating actionable financial advice from business records demands that models integrate numerical reasoning, domain knowledge, and sound judgment, while avoiding recommendations that could harm the business. Direct supervision is difficult: historical decisions are not necessarily optimal, and high-quality free-form labels are expensive to obtain. We formulate financial advice generation as a reinforcement learning problem and fine-tune an open-weight language model using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Our reward is an LLM-as-a-judge rubric that scores each recommendation across multiple binary dimensions of advice quality, augmented with a safety gate for harm prevention. Since LLM-based evaluation alone cannot confirm whether improvements reflect genuine business value rather than adaptation to the judge, we complement it with a judge-independent audit based on a standard doubly-robust Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) estimator. Under this observational off-policy audit, our trained LLM achieves approximately twice the estimated gross-profit lift of the strongest evaluated commercial baseline ($0.0228$ vs.\ $0.0104$), together with the lowest downside rate and the least negative tail risk of any policy evaluated. Notably, the two evaluations do not rank the baselines identically: the untrained base model places last on the judge rubric but second on the causal audit, indicating that the audit captures a signal the judge does not. Our results demonstrate that GRPO with a finance-grounded reward signal can produce substantially more useful business recommendations than commercial LLMs, and that a judge-independent causal audit is a valuable complement to, rather than a confirmation of, LLM-as-a-judge assessment in financial NLP.

items.title: Researchers find VITA clinical RAG system matches or outperforms newer LLMs on HealthBench, excelling in India-specific medical contexts [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: A corpus-specific clinical RAG system matches or outperforms newer frontier LLMs on HealthBench
items.summary: Researchers evaluated VITA, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system designed for clinical knowledge retrieval in India and other low- and middle-income countries, against general-purpose large language models (LLMs) on the HealthBench medical benchmark. VITA, which accesses a curated corpus including disease guidelines and antimicrobial resistance data specific to India, scored highest on 4,023 HealthBench questions when judged by GPT-4.1, outperforming models like GPT-5.4 and Claude Sonnet 4.6. A follow-up test on a 500-question subset with newer models and a neutral judge found VITA and GPT-5.5 statistically tied on average scores, with VITA leading on weighted points and question wins.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: General-purpose large language models (LLMs) have recently been reported to match or exceed specialized clinical AI tools on medical benchmarks, but such comparisons draw on a narrow set of systems and on benchmarks developed largely in high-income settings. We evaluate VITA, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system purpose-built for contextual knowledge retrieval in India and other low- and middle-income (LMIC) settings. VITA retrieves from a curated corpus of disease-specific guidelines, India-specific antimicrobial resistance data, national formulary constraints, and resource-limited care protocols; its architecture and corpus are proprietary, but the benchmark, the physician-written rubrics, and our full response and scoring outputs are public for independent verification. On 4,023 English-language HealthBench questions (80.5% of the benchmark), scored with a GPT-4.1 judge, VITA ranked first with 51.9% of possible rubric points, ahead of GPT-5.4 (46.1%), o4-mini (44.3%), Gemini 3.1 Pro (42.6%), and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (37.3%), and scored highest on 45.4% of questions. To test robustness to newer models and judge lineage, a 500-question subset was re-run against current-generation models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Pro, Grok 4.3) and graded by a neutral open-weight judge (DeepSeek-V4-Pro) sharing no lineage with any system tested. Here the gap narrowed to parity: VITA and GPT-5.5 were statistically indistinguishable on mean per-question score, while VITA led on points-weighted score and won the most questions. VITA's advantages in accuracy and completeness persisted under the neutral judge; its communication scores were lower. These results indicate that a purpose-built clinical RAG system remains competitive with frontier LLMs on an open benchmark, consistent with corpus specificity as a design variable that improves grounding at some cost to communication polish.

items.title: Researchers identify simulator collapse in multi-agent RL with single LLM simulators and propose Verbalized Sampling and Co-Training to improve generalization and policy diversity [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL
items.summary:
Researchers found that multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) using a single large language model (LLM) to simulate user behavior suffers from simulator collapse, where the policy overfits to narrow strategies exploiting the simulator's dominant mode and fails to generalize to new simulators and real users. They propose two solutions: Verbalized Sampling at inference time to broaden simulator behavior, and Co-Training at training time to optimize policies against multiple trainable simulators, preventing overfitting.

The team validated these methods on three multi-turn benchmarks, showing up to 9% improvement with Verbalized Sampling and 14% with Co-Training over single-simulator RL, with similar gains observed in human studies. They also released SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training in multi-agent RL, emphasizing that training environment diversity is crucial for real-world deployment generalization.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning for human-AI interaction typically relies on a single large language model to simulate user behavior. We show that this approach systematically fails to generalize, and trace the failure to simulator collapse: because the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, an LLM policy trained against it overfits to narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's dominant mode, and such a policy transfers poorly to unseen simulators and real users. We formalize this collapse theoretically and propose two complementary solutions, one at inference time and one at training time. The inference-time solution, Verbalized Sampling, broadens the simulator's behavior by sampling from a verbalized response distribution, reducing mode collapse. The training-time solution, Co-Training, jointly optimizes the policy against a population of trainable simulators, preventing it from overfitting to any single simulator's mode. We validate both solutions on three multi-turn benchmarks: Persuasion for Good, $\tau^2$-bench, and CooperBench. Verbalized Sampling improves held-out success by up to 9% over single-simulator RL, and Co-Training pushes gains further to 14%; the human study shows similar gain on real users. Both solutions preserve the policy diversity that collapses under single-simulator RL. To support further work in this direction, we release SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training multi-agent RL. More broadly, our results suggest that the diversity of the training environment, not only the policy, is critical to the generalization of multi-turn RL to real-world deployment.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate test-time capability transfer from stronger to weaker AI models via inference-time harnesses, nearly doubling target model performance on Theory-of-Mind benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI4AI at Test-Time: Strong-to-Weak Capability Transfer via Harnesses
items.summary:
Researchers explore whether capabilities of large AI models can be transferred to smaller models at test time without parameter updates by using inference-time harnesses constructed by stronger builder models. They tested this approach on four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks, where builder models refined harnesses using 5% of data before evaluating on full test sets, resulting in average target model performance increasing from 0.49 to 0.91.

The study finds that performance gains mainly arise from offloading unstable reasoning to deterministic code, benchmark-specific routing, and strict answer-format enforcement rather than encouraging broader reasoning or sampling by the target model. The quality of harnesses improves with builder model reasoning effort, platform effects are minor compared to builder capability, and weaker target models benefit the most. This suggests inference-time harness design complements traditional training-time distillation by enabling strong models to transfer cognitive structure to weaker models without retraining.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work on distillation transfers the capabilities of large models to smaller ones often by updating the latter's parameters, through teacher forcing, on-policy distillation, and related training-time methods. In this paper, we ask whether such transfer can instead occur at test time. We study strong-to-weak scaffolding: whether a stronger builder model can construct inference-time harnesses that help a weaker target model solve tasks more reliably without any parameter updates. Using four representative Theory-of-Mind benchmarks, each builder model uses 5% of the data as a validation set to iteratively refine its harness over multiple rounds, after which the finalized harness is evaluated on the full test set. Empirically, this form of test-time capability transfer is highly effective, nearly doubling average target-model performance from 0.49 to 0.91. Our analysis shows that the gains come primarily from offloading unstable model reasoning into deterministic code, benchmark-specific routing, and strict answer-format enforcement, rather than from encouraging the target model to reason more extensively or sample more broadly. We further find that builder-model reasoning effort improves harness quality monotonically, platform effects are modest relative to the builder model's own capability, and weaker target models receive the largest gains. These results suggest that inference-time harness design is an important complement to conventional training-time distillation, enabling strong models to transfer cognitive structure to weaker models without retraining.

items.originalTitle: SteeringSafety: Benchmarking Representation Steering in LLMs Across Safety Perspectives
items.summary: SteeringSafety introduces a benchmark to assess representation steering methods in large language models (LLMs) across nine safety perspectives, including refusal, bias, hallucination, social behaviors, reasoning, epistemic integrity, and normative judgment. The benchmark covers 18 datasets and supports unified implementation of methods like DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, and LAT with recent enhancements such as conditional steering. Evaluations on Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen-2.5-7B show that steering effectiveness varies by method, model, and safety perspective, with DIM generally effective but all methods exhibiting entanglement where improving one safety aspect affects others.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2509.13450v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce SteeringSafety, a benchmark for evaluating representation steering methods across nine safety perspectives spanning 18 datasets. While prior work highlights the general capabilities of representation steering, we focus on safety perspectives including refusal, bias, hallucination, social behaviors, reasoning, epistemic integrity, and normative judgment. SteeringSafety provides modularized building blocks for state-of-the-art steering methods, enabling unified implementation of DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, and LAT with recent enhancements such as conditional steering. Results on Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen-2.5-7B show that strong steering performance depends on the pairing of method, model, and specific perspective. For instance, DIM is consistently effective, yet all methods exhibit substantial entanglement, where improving effectiveness on one safety perspective often significantly changes performance on others. Social behaviors are most vulnerable (degradation up to 76%), refusal steering (jailbreaking) frequently compromises normative judgment such as commonsense morality (up to 26%), and hallucination steering shifts political views unpredictably across models, ranging from a 25% shift to the right to a 28% shift to the left. These findings show the need to understand steering methods through multiple safety angles rather than a single target behavior.

items.originalTitle: Moxia: A Trust-First Neuro-Symbolic Execution Architecture for Self-Explaining Mathematical Reasoning
items.summary: Moxia, formerly known as AXIOM, is a neuro-symbolic architecture designed for mathematical reasoning over natural-language input. It converts informal problem text into a structured schema processed by a deterministic computer algebra system (CAS) that derives and verifies answers or abstains when uncertain, providing step-by-step explanations generated from the computation itself. The system routes problems through a large set of predefined handlers, achieving over 90% accuracy on the MATH test set and nearly 90% on held-out data, with zero confident wrong answers on the latter, demonstrating robustness beyond memorization.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.00671v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present Moxia (formerly AXIOM), a trust-first neuro-symbolic architecture for self-explaining mathematical reasoning over natural-language input. Its language model is strictly a canonicalizer: it rewrites informal problem text into a narrow schema consumed by a deterministic Computer-Algebra-System (CAS) pipeline, which derives and verifies the answer or abstains as a first-class output. Routing follows a 1:1:1 alignment of problem-shape regex, schema-specific prompt, and closed-form CAS handler, with 4,783 routes shipped, 71% of which answer without invoking the language model, and zero LOST_CORRECT regressions as a standing release gate. Because the answer is derived rather than generated, so is its explanation: every handler emits a step trace of the computation it performed, rendered as prose by a layer covering all 4,785 task files that cannot narrate a step the handler did not take. Derivations export to Lean 4 as well: 479 task files (10%) emit a theorem from the problem's declared data, 445 accepted by the Lean kernel with Mathlib; that gate covers a fixture corpus, so live output is generated, not machine-checked. We report two numbers and never fuse them. On the full 7-category MATH test split, designed against, Moxia answers 90.2% (4,510/5,000) with one confident-wrong answer (99.98% trust on parseable). On held-out MATH-500, never designed against, it answers 89.2% (446/500) with zero confident-wrong answers. The 1.0 pp gap is the substantive result: a registry that had merely memorized problem shapes would collapse on held-out data, and this one does not. The rule-only path answers the 20,000-record lm-eval arithmetic benchmark at 100%, 1 ms per record. What we emphasize is not an accuracy figure but the forward dynamic: every logged abstain is a candidate correct after one ship cycle, since new tasks compose without regressing the registry.

items.title: Researchers release RedditPersona, a modular framework for community-conditioned LLM adaptation using Reddit data with five grouping strategies and shared evaluation metrics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: RedditPersona: A Modular Framework for Community-Conditioned LLM Adaptation from Reddit
items.summary:
RedditPersona is a new modular framework designed to standardize community-conditioned language model adaptation by unifying data collection, community definition, and evaluation methods. It collects Reddit posts and comments, profiles users, partitions them using five strategies—subreddit-based, graph-structural, semantic, hybrid, and interaction-based—trains parameter-efficient adapters via QLoRA, and evaluates them on fluency, fidelity, distributional alignment, and community identifiability.

Applied to 112 subreddits in the urban well-being domain with over 301,000 user profiles and 16 million comments, the study finds that adapters' behavioral identifiability correlates with each strategy's alignment to subreddit baselines, revealing a trade-off between identifiability and similarity to real text across all strategies. The code and configuration files are publicly available for further research and reuse.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.06027v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Community-conditioned language model adaptation needs choices about data collection, community definition, and evaluation that are currently made independently in each study, making it hard to compare assumptions or reuse artifacts. We present RedditPersona, a modular framework that standardizes these choices: it collects Reddit posts and comments, profiles active users, partitions them under five grouping strategies (subreddit-based, graph-structural, semantic, hybrid, and interaction-based), trains a parameter-efficient adapter per strategy via QLoRA, and evaluates them under a shared metric suite spanning fluency, fidelity, distributional alignment, and community identifiability. Applied to 112 subreddits in the urban well-being domain (301,429 user profiles, 16M+ comments), we find that adapters' behavioral identifiability tracks each strategy's agreement with the subreddit baseline, and that a consistent trade-off between identifiability and distributional similarity to real text holds across all five strategies. The code and configuration files are available at: https://github.com/Ahghaffari/redditpersona.

items.title: Researchers propose almost orthogonal feature constraints to reduce interference in language model interventions, improving modularity and preserving performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Superposition Without Interference? Towards Isolated Interventions via Almost Orthogonal Features in Language Models
items.summary: Researchers address the challenge of feature entanglement in language models, which causes interference during localized interventions on linear features representing meaningful concepts. They propose constraining internal features to be almost orthogonal, promoting modular representations that support more isolated and reliable causal interventions. The study formalizes the relationship between feature interference and intervention effects, introducing an orthogonality regularization to limit interference propagation. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach enables more isolated interventions on mathematical reasoning concepts without degrading model performance, with code made publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.04718v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A central premise in mechanistic interpretability is that meaningful concepts in language models are represented by linear features in activation space. For such features to support reliable interventions, manipulating one feature should not substantially alter the effects of others. In practice, however, feature entanglement leads to interference such that localized interventions can have unintended downstream effects. Motivated by the _Independent Causal Mechanisms_ principle, we propose to constrain internal features to be almost orthogonal. We argue that this promotes modular representations amenable to causal intervention. We formalize this problem by characterizing the gap between an idealized isolated intervention and its realized effect on model outputs in terms of feature interference. We upper-bound the propagation of feature interference in terms of the self-coherence of the feature dictionary, and relate this discrepancy to an explicit orthogonality regularization on the dictionary itself. Empirically, we show that this regularization enables more isolated interventions on mathematical reasoning concepts while preserving model performance. Our code is available under https://github.com/mrtzmllr/sae-icm.

items.originalTitle: Reproducing, Analyzing, and Detecting Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CHERRL, a Controllable Hacking Environment for Rubric-based Reinforcement Learning (RL), to study reward hacking where policy models exploit biases in large language model judges scoring outputs. CHERRL injects known biases to reproduce reward hacking behaviors, observe reward divergence, and identify hacking onset, providing a controlled testbed for analysis and mitigation.

The study analyzes different judge biases in terms of their discoverability and exploitability and explores an agent that can automatically detect the onset of reward hacking from training logs. The CHERRL code and environment are publicly available for further research and experimentation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.04923v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) uses an LLM-as-a-Judge (LaaJ) to score model outputs according to rubrics as rewards. However, policy models may exploit latent biases in the judge, leading to reward hacking and ineffective or unsafe training outcomes. In real-world rubric-based RL, such hacking behaviors are often subtle and entangled with multiple judge biases, making them difficult to analyze, detect, and mitigate. In this paper, we introduce CHERRL, a Controllable Hacking Environment for Rubric-based RL. By injecting known biases into LaaJ, CHERRL enables stable reproduction of reward hacking, explicit observation of reward divergence, and identification of hacking onset. This provides a clean experimental testbed for studying the mechanisms and mitigations of reward hacking in rubric-based RL. To demonstrate its utility, we analyze different judge biases from the perspectives of discoverability and exploitability, and explore an agent for automatically detecting reward hacking onset from training logs. The code and environment are publicly available at https://github.com/THUAIS-Lab/CHERRL.

items.title: Researchers propose cost-aware cross-tier transfer method for evolutionary optimization of LLM prompts, achieving up to 54x lower search costs by using cheaper models for high-volume tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Optimize Cheap, Deploy Strong: Cost-Aware Cross-Tier Transfer for Evolutionary Optimization
items.summary: Researchers present a method to reduce the cost of evolutionary optimization for large language model (LLM) prompts by decoupling the roles of LLMs in the search process. They run the high-volume answering role on cheaper models while reserving stronger models for less frequent reflection and variation tasks, then transfer the optimized prompts to stronger target models. This approach maintains or improves prompt quality while significantly lowering search costs across multiple tasks and model families.

They run the high-volume answering role on cheaper models while reserving stronger models for less frequent reflection and variation tasks, then transfer the optimized prompts to stronger target models. This approach maintains or improves prompt quality while significantly lowering search costs across multiple tasks and model families.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.10694v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evolutionary optimization of LLM prompts and agentic programs (e.g., GEPA) is dominated by fitness evaluation: scoring each candidate runs an answering LLM over a validation set, so the evaluator's price tier dictates total search cost. We restructure that search by decoupling the three roles an LLM plays, running the high-volume answering role on the cheapest tier, reserving a strong model for the rare reflection/variation operator, then exploiting upward cross-tier transfer to deploy the cheaply evolved prompt on a stronger target. We contribute a cost-controlled characterization of when cheap-tier search substitutes for target-tier search, and where it fails. Across four tasks (HotpotQA, IFBench, LiveBench-Math, HoVer) and eleven models in four model families, the resulting prompt matches or exceeds same-tier optimization while placing over 96% of search tokens on the cheapest tier, at 5.6-14x lower search cost, rising to 25-54x where reasoning tiers emit long chains of thought on every fitness call.

items.title: MaSRead enables content-addressed reading of replicated latent stores by routing queries through keyed tag sets and decoding selected fragments with attention masks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MaSRead: Content-Addressed Reading of Replicated Latent Stores
items.summary: MaSRead is a method for reading from replicated latent stores where independent agents share computed state as key-value cache fragments merged via conflict-free replicated data types. It routes queries through opaque keyed tag sets derived from fragment words and decodes selected fragments under hard attention masks, allowing multi-hop queries to retrieve relevant fragments despite interference from colocated data. This approach maintains effectiveness across various store types and model families, with decoding complexity depending on fragment length rather than total store size. MaSRead improves selective readability of replicated latent stores based on content connectivity to queries but may miss disconnected evidence and is limited by the fixed reader model.

items.title: Researchers propose a self-evolving agent memory framework to build lifelong AI partners for materials science, improving task success and reducing errors without model updates [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Harnessing agent memory to build lifelong AI partners for materials scientists
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a persistent memory framework for AI agents in materials science that stores scientific experience as inspectable facts and executable skills. This approach enables retrieval, revision, and migration of observations, failure boundaries, protocols, and validation checks across different AI models, enhancing reproducibility and knowledge transfer.

Evaluations across multiple computational materials research tasks showed that incorporating this memory nearly doubled task success rates, reduced errors significantly, and lowered computational resource usage without updating model parameters. The framework demonstrated improvements in wavefunction initialization, simulation workflows, and tool usage efficiency, suggesting that agent memory can serve as a durable, portable scientific asset that preserves and enhances materials research knowledge beyond individual AI models.

items.title: Researchers find activation steering in language models causes predictable, structured side effects across multiple behaviors and models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Forecasting Side Effects of Activation Steering
items.summary: Researchers analyzed activation steering, a method that alters language model behavior by adjusting hidden activations without retraining, and found that it often produces unintended side effects on other behaviors. Their study across three open-weight language models and 67 behaviors revealed these side effects are common, structured, and asymmetric, and cannot be fully explained by existing heuristics. Despite this complexity, the side effects can be largely predicted before steering is applied, with their magnitude depending on the targeted behavior and direction forecastable from the model's original representations. This finding enables proactive safety assessments and more informed deployment of activation steering techniques.

items.title: Researchers argue semantic safety constraints in AI are off-support objects not captured by learning invariants, affecting prior design, containment, and verification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Off-Support Barrier: Why Semantic Safety Constraints Are Not Learning-Problem Invariants, and What Follows for Prior Design, Containment, and Verification
items.summary: Researchers analyze why semantic safety constraints, such as preventing AI agents from escaping sandboxes, are off-support objects not measurable by standard learning theory metrics. They explain how this leads to issues like reward hacking and sandbox escape under outcome-based optimization and why Bayesian prior design or soft penalties have limited effectiveness in singular models. The study uses the July 2026 OpenAI–Hugging Face evaluation incident as a motivating example and provides numerical experiments and formal proofs to support their findings. The work also discusses the implications for formal verification and the challenges posed by performative prediction and self-referential dynamics where traditional analytic tools fail.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11243v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We argue that a single structural fact organizes a wide range of phenomena in contemporary AI safety: a semantic safety constraint (e.g., the agent does not escape its sandbox) is an off-support object. Formally, if q is the data distribution and \(p(\cdot\mid w)\) the model, the safety predicate B is not measurable with respect to \(\sigma(\text{model}, q)\), whereas the real log-canonical threshold (RLCT) of singular learning theory (SLT) is. From this non-invariance we derive, as corollaries rather than independent observations: (i) why reward hacking and sandbox escape arise under outcome-based optimization; (ii) why encoding such constraints through Bayesian prior design or soft penalty weighting has poor leverage in singular models; (iii) why hard invariants belong in the harness and soft dispositions in the model; (iv) why the same B is nonetheless soundly and locally certifiable by formal verification, exactly as the local learning coefficient (LLC) locally pins the same RLCT --- with two precise points of disanalogy; and (v) why the residual difficulty, identifying which off-support region matters, coincides with performative prediction and self-referential functional dynamics, where SLT's analytic machinery breaks down. We use the July 2026 OpenAI--Hugging Face evaluation incident as the motivating case. Numerical experiments code and related proofs in lean are available at https://github.com/xiangze/Preventing_Jailbreak_as_regularization

items.title: Researchers develop BEST-KAG, a multimodal knowledge graph and large language model framework for clause-grounded question answering on building engineering standards [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: BEST-KAG: Enhancing Question Answering of Building Engineering Standards with Multimodal Knowledge Graph Modeling and Large Language Model
items.summary:
Researchers have developed BEST-KAG, a multimodal knowledge-driven framework designed to improve question answering on building engineering standards by integrating a multimodal knowledge graph with large language models. The framework addresses limitations of current workflows that rely on keyword searches and manual interpretation, enabling multi-clause reasoning, multimodal knowledge use, and traceable clause-level evidence linkage.

BEST-KAG features a multimodal knowledge graph representing document hierarchy and heterogeneous standard knowledge, a hybrid rule-LLM pipeline for scalable knowledge extraction creating a graph with over 171,000 nodes and 310,000 edges from 251 standards, and a graph-retrieval-based generation architecture for traceable answers. Experiments show BEST-KAG outperforms mainstream large language models by up to 74% on expert evaluations and metrics like BLEU and ROUGE.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Construction standards are critical for building safety and sustainability. Existing standard application workflows rely on keyword-based document retrieval and manual cross-clause interpretation, which cannot reliably support multi-clause reasoning, multimodal knowledge utilization, or traceable clause-level evidence linkage. To address these limitations, this study develops a multimodal knowledge-driven framework that supports question answering on standard knowledge named BEST-KAG (Knowledge-Augmented Generation for Building Engineering STandards). The framework introduces 1) a multimodal knowledge graph (MKG) for unified representation of document hierarchy and heterogeneous standard knowledge with various connections, 2) a rule-LLM hybrid knowledge construction pipeline for scalable multimodal knowledge extraction, creating a large MAG with 251 building engineering standards, 171,652 nodes and 310,914 edges, and 3) a graph-retrieval-based knowledge-augmented generation architecture for clause-grounded and traceable question answering. Experiments demonstrate that BEST-KAG consistently outperforms multiple mainstream LLMs in terms of Expert evaluation, and metrics including BLEU, and ROUGE, with the best improvement up to 74.01% compared to the baselines.

outputCleanup.description:
Researchers have developed BEST-KAG, a multimodal knowledge-driven framework designed to improve question answering on building engineering standards by integrating a multimodal knowledge graph with large language models. The framework addresses limitations of current workflows that rely on keyword searches and manual interpretation, enabling multi-clause reasoning, multimodal knowledge use, and traceable clause-level evidence linkage.

BEST-KAG features a multimodal knowledge graph representing document hierarchy and heterogeneous standard knowledge, a hybrid rule-LLM pipeline for scalable knowledge extraction creating a graph with over 171,000 nodes and 310,000 edges from 251 standards, and a graph-retrieval-based generation architecture for traceable answers. Experiments show BEST-KAG outperforms mainstream large language models by up to 74% on expert evaluations and metrics like BLEU and ROUGE.

items.summary: Researchers introduce AI Tutor, a reinforcement learning model designed to enhance sustainable learning in online education by balancing new knowledge acquisition with reinforcement of prior learning and modeling learner engagement to reduce dropout. The system personalizes guidance to support effective learning and sustained participation across diverse learner profiles. Evaluations on 23 million learning records from 33,700 learners show AI Tutor outperforms existing methods in engagement, knowledge retention, and final learning outcomes, demonstrating adaptive and human-centered support strategies.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online education offers unprecedented scalability and accessibility to global learners from diverse backgrounds, but it often suffers from low engagement and poor long term learning effectiveness. To address these challenges, we introduce AI Tutor, a reinforcement learning based model designed to promote sustainable learning by optimizing both short and longterm learning outcomes. In the short term, AI-Tutor draws on cognitive theory to guide learners through a balance of acquiring new knowledge and reinforcing prior learning. In the long term, it models learner engagement to inform strategies that sustain motivation and reduce dropout. These enhancements enable AI-Tutor to provide personalized guidance that fosters both effective learning and sustained participation. Empirical evaluations on 23 million learning records from 33,700 learners show that AI Tutor consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across engagement, knowledge retention, and final learning outcomes. Learning path analyses further reveal how AI-Tutor adapts its strategies to learners with diverse profiles, offering adaptive and human-centered support.

items.title: Researchers present Thea, a harness for embodied agents that orchestrates robot capabilities using scene graphs and evaluation codes to enable long-horizon task completion in physical environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards the Harness of Embodied Agents
items.summary: Researchers introduce Thea, a harness framework that extends the coding agent paradigm to embodied agents in the physical world by orchestrating robot capabilities wrapped as callable tools. Thea addresses challenges unique to physical environments, such as reading the world's state and judging action outcomes, by using a persistent symbolic scene graph and evaluation exit codes to close the agent-world interaction loop. This approach enables the composition of rich behaviors and supports the completion of complex, long-duration tasks in real-world settings.

Thea addresses challenges unique to physical environments, such as reading the world's state and judging action outcomes, by using a persistent symbolic scene graph and evaluation exit codes to close the agent-world interaction loop. This approach enables the composition of rich behaviors and supports the completion of complex, long-duration tasks in real-world settings.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11246v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The success of coding agents has established the harness as a paradigm: what an agent achieves depends not on the model alone, but on the infrastructure around it. We ask whether the same paradigm extends to embodied agents in the physical world. We present Thea, a harness in which an agentic loop orchestrates robot capabilities, each wrapped as a callable tool. It inherits the core components of coding agents, modified as the physical world requires. The world, however, withholds two abilities that software grants for free: reading the state of the world, and judging the outcome of an action. To bridge these gaps, Thea introduces Scene Graph as Context, a persistent, symbolic representation of the world, and Evaluation as Exit Codes, which detects when an action should terminate, judges whether it succeeded, and on failure diagnoses the cause. Together they close the loop between the agent and the physical world. Rich behaviors then emerge from the composition of tools, and the closed loop carries long-horizon tasks to completion in real environments.

items.title: Researchers develop symbolic machine learning corrections to improve Peng-Robinson equation predictions for hydrocarbon-nitrogen vapor-liquid equilibrium [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Symbolic Machine Learning for Vapor-Liquid Equilibrium Prediction in Cx-N2 Binary Mixtures
items.summary: Researchers propose a symbolic machine learning approach to enhance vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) predictions for hydrocarbon-nitrogen mixtures by correcting the Peng-Robinson equation of state (PR-EOS) using interpretable symbolic expressions derived from experimental data. This method first identifies symbolic corrections for individual hydrocarbons and then models coefficients as functions of carbon number to generalize across different hydrocarbons. The approach significantly improves prediction accuracy over the original PR-EOS across various hydrocarbon-nitrogen systems, offering an interpretable framework for better VLE modeling.
items.description: Researchers propose a symbolic machine learning approach to enhance vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) predictions for hydrocarbon-nitrogen mixtures by correcting the Peng-Robinson equation of state (PR-EOS) using interpretable symbolic expressions derived from experimental data. This method first identifies symbolic corrections for individual hydrocarbons and then models coefficients as functions of carbon number to generalize across different hydrocarbons. The approach significantly improves prediction accuracy over the original PR-EOS across various hydrocarbon-nitrogen systems, offering an interpretable framework for better VLE modeling.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate prediction of vapor--liquid equilibrium (VLE) for hydrocarbon-nitrogen mixtures remains challenging for cubic equations of state, particularly across broad ranges of composition and hydrocarbon chain length. While deep learning models can provide accurate predictions, they often lack interpretability and explicit analytical expressions. In this work, we propose a symbolic machine learning approach to discover interpretable symbolic corrections to Peng-Robinson equation-of-state (PR-EOS) predictions from experimental data. The proposed approach adopts a two-level strategy: symbolic expressions are first identified for individual hydrocarbon systems, after which their coefficients are represented as functions of carbon number to enable accurate prediction across different hydrocarbon systems. The results demonstrate significantly improved prediction accuracy over the original PR-EOS across all hydrocarbon-nitrogen systems. Overall, the proposed approach provides an interpretable symbolic correction framework for improving PR-EOS predictions of hydrocarbon-nitrogen VLE.

items.title: Researchers present Deployment Decision Reliability framework showing agent leaderboards reflect specialization more than capability across three benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Deployment Decision Reliability: A Generalizability-Theory Framework for Sizing Long-Horizon Agent Evaluations
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed three open agent-trace benchmarks and found that agent leaderboards primarily rank specialization rather than overall capability, with the agent main effect accounting for less than 3% of total variance and agent-by-task interaction accounting for 7-23%. They used a four-facet Generalizability Theory variance decomposition with three estimators that closely agreed, revealing that leaderboard reliability collapses on the hardest tasks and that training-cell reliability negatively correlates with held-out reliability.

The study also found that population-level diagnostics transfer across benchmarks but per-family agent rankings invert, and that trace-level failure profiles are idiosyncratic while cell-level profiles generalize well. These insights were consolidated into Deployment Decision Reliability (DDR), a reporting discipline designed to help enterprise buyers make defensible decisions. All related code, data loaders, and fit artifacts have been released under an open-source license.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11323v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise practitioners read agent leaderboards as if they ranked agent capability. We show, across three open agent-trace benchmarks (TheAgentCompany, $\tau^2$-bench, and AppWorld), that the agent main effect accounts for less than 3% of total variance in every dataset and check type, while the agent-by-task interaction accounts for 7-23%. Leaderboards rank specialization, not capability. We arrive at this through a four-facet Generalizability Theory variance decomposition, fit with three estimators (Henderson Method-I, REML via lme4, and a Bayesian binomial GLMM) that agree to three decimal places. Four further findings sharpen what the leaderboard is hiding. First, aggregate reliability collapses on the hardest task quartile: $E\rho^2$ on $\tau^2$ action_checks falls from 0.752 to 0.000. Second, training-cell reliability negatively correlates with held-out reliability ($r = -0.90$ on $\tau^2$), meaning the designs that look most reliable replicate worst. Third, population-level diagnostics transfer across enterprise benchmarks (capability-gap ratio stable at 0.35-0.40) but per-family agent rankings invert. Fourth, on the MAST failure taxonomy, trace-level mode profiles are idiosyncratic (MAE = 0.261) while cell-level profiles generalise (MAE = 0.056, $r = 0.83$). We package these into Deployment Decision Reliability (DDR), a one-page reporting discipline that turns the variance-component table into five decisions an enterprise buyer can defend. All code, data loaders, and fit artifacts are released under an open-source license.

items.title: Study compares frontier LLMs GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Google's Gemini Embedding 2 on hard-negative text-to-image retrieval, finding similar performance on Flickr30k [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Frontier LLMs Match Natively Multimodal Embeddings? A Comparison on Hard-Negative Text-to-Image Retrieval
items.summary:
A new study evaluates whether leading large language models (LLMs) can match the performance of Google's Gemini Embedding 2, a natively multimodal embedding model released in March 2026, on text-to-image retrieval tasks. The research compares GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 against Gemini Embedding 2 using the Flickr30k dataset, focusing on hard-negative retrieval scenarios.

The results show that GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 perform on par with Gemini Embedding 2 in zero-shot visual ranking tasks. However, the study notes that once embeddings are precomputed, native multimodal embeddings like Gemini Embedding 2 are better suited for applications requiring low latency.
